Baby D

[MOTHER OF BABY D] (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS

Just before the jury come in, Mr Myers, I think the difficulties that arose yesterday have all been resolved.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I hope they have.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We are grateful to all, including your Lordship and the court, for the assistance with that. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm very grateful in particular to the officer here, who has facilitated this and assisted greatly. I've asked that my thanks be passed to you and to those with whom you have been communicating.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed. And she has a desk now as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Jury in, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Yes, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, your Lordship will remember that we're now moving to the case of [Baby D], which is count 4, and we will start by calling [Baby D]'s mother, [Mother of Baby D], please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [MOTHER OF BABY D] (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could we start by you telling the jury your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: [Mother of Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you. [Mother of Baby D], sometimes it's difficult when you're sitting down to keep your voice up, but even though the questions are coming from me initially and then from Mr Myers here after me, could you try to give your answers to the jury, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Sure.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And please just ignore the microphone that's in front of you: it'll be your natural voice that we all have to hear. So make a real effort because if you drop your voice, you simply have to repeat what you've said, which is not helpful for you and of course it just prolongs the proceedings. So I'll keep prompting you if I need to: I'm not being rude, I'm just making sure for the jury. If anyone can't hear, just raise a hand. That's the rule that we have. If anyone can't hear they raise a hand so we can see. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Is your husband [Father of Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you marry [Father of Baby D] back in September 2014?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you discover that you were pregnant in about October of 2014?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And did you suffer from nausea and sickness at the beginning of your pregnancy, but thereafter were you fairly well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you. As a result of parenting lessons that you went to, did you develop a concern about your waters breaking?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And as a result, did you buy a mattress protector?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Your concern, to that degree at least, was well-founded because in the early hours of 18 June 2015, did you wake up in effect in a damp patch at about 3.30 in the morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you phone the hospital as a result of that, the maternity hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did they tell you to monitor the situation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you continue to rest until about 9 o'clock that morning on 18 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not exactly rest, but I waited.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, okay. At about 9.30, did you ring the hospital again and were you told to go into the hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: By that stage were you 36 weeks plus 6 days pregnant, as far as you were aware?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: 36 plus 5, I believe.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 36 plus 5, all right. In any event, whichever's exactly right, you were about that far advanced. And did you go to the hospital with your husband and arrive at the Countess of Chester Hospital at about 11.30 on the morning of 18 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. That's right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you explain to the hospital that you thought your waters had broken?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And did the staff at the hospital in effect confirm that your suspicion was correct?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: They confirmed. They didn't test, but they confirmed, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Did they then monitor you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. They checked the baby and myself. Not for very long.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You are speaking very softly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's all right, it's natural, particularly when you're being asked questions by someone who's close to you. Perhaps if you could just face that way, Mr Johnson won't mind. Not for very long, you said?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not for very long.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: They checked you, but not for very long?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And did you speak to a nurse at that stage --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- do you remember?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was that particular nurse -- did you identify her subsequently in a statement as -- I think you gave numbers to the nurses, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you give her a number ad did you refer to her as nurse number 3, do you remember?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Um... I would have said nurse number 1. I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. If you can't remember, it doesn't matter, don't worry about it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. Were you scanned at that stage or not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Were you in effect sent home after being examined?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that was 18 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the 19th did you return to the hospital or not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. In the morning, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you see a midwife when you got to the hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you examined and were various checks and measurements performed on you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. Not straightaway. I had to wait.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you express a concern to the staff at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And what was your concern by that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Well, I broke my waters for more than 24 hours. I felt I haven't rested a lot, I didn't feel right, the baby didn't seem to move as well. I was concerned for infection because I hadn't been given any antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was the decision then taken to try to induce your labour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Initially, was that done by giving you a pessary?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: One pessary at first, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That didn't work. Were you given a second one?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, I believe 6 hours after, instead of 4.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that was delayed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And what was the impression you got as to the reason for the delay?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: They were very busy. I thought they forgot about me.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you then given -- put on to an intravenous drip in order to induce your labour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not for many hours. Not until the following days -- day, sorry.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was it at about, as far as you recall, 2.25 in the morning of 20 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, so very, very delayed because it should have been 4 hours between each stage.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. By that stage I think you calculated that it had been about 46 or 47 hours or so since you had felt that your waters had broken at home?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Roughly, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: How did you feel at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Very worried, scared. I felt unwell and not in control and a bit forgotten by the staff, really.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At one stage did you go to the bathroom?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And did you notice that there was some blood coming out of you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And did that cause you concern?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. I was on my own. My husband let me go because I asked to have some time. I was probably getting very grumpy and very tired and had not really rested the whole 2 days. I was starting to feel quite a bit of pain, labour has clearly started, and yes, there was blood in the toilet, so I went back and I asked for someone to do something.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then did you see a doctor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. I can't remember which, but yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think you described the doctor to the police, although you didn't know her name; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Mm-hm, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And was your description that you thought that she was possibly Indian, possibly mixed race, and aged somewhere in her late 20s, early 30s?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You thought she was about 170 centimetres tall and was a slim or skinny build with dark, curly hair, tied up?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was she the first doctor that you had seen since you had arrived at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you assessed by that doctor and told that essentially both you and [Baby D] were okay and that you needed to wait to see if [Baby D] could be delivered naturally?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. She didn't really speak to me that much, she spoke with the midwives. They looked at the notes and at the end, when they were done talking, she just said, "You'll be fine, we'll try and see if this can happen naturally", and that's that.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And were you told at that stage that your position would be reviewed in a further 4 hours, which would have taken you to about 11 o'clock that morning on the 20th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 11 o'clock were you assessed again?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was this by a different doctor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Different doctor.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And this doctor was a man?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was he a white man?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You got the impression from his accent that he wasn't British; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Probably German, I would go with.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and you are French?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you thought he was German. There you were in an English hospital with a German doctor as you thought.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. But like you, what was his English like?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Great. No problem. I think we understood each other, no problem.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you describe him as being in his early 40s and -- I think your words were very tall at 6 feet tall?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: He was a big guy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Big that way as well as that way (indicating)?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Like (indicating) big height, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So a well-built man?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Well-built guy, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Did he examine you?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did he record the fact that really there had been, without going into the detail, little progress so far as your labour was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: He was a lot more friendly and I think he was the first professional in the hospital that actually spoke to me and exchanged with me and addressed my concern then, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you at that stage enquire of him whether a caesarean section might be considered as the means of delivery for [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I think we were in 50 hours then, so, yes, I asked if that was going to be something we consider because there was no progress and there was no dilation, no nothing going towards delivery naturally.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you say there was no dilation?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So you were examined?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: He physically examined, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Did the German doctor explain to you that a Csection wasn't an easy option so far as you were concerned?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I think he was trying to put me off it. Yes, he was just trying to say we've got to try naturally, you're young, you're healthy. I think sometimes people think this is an easy option, the C-section, which for me was the last resort. So that was not for me the case. But he said we should try, wait and see how we go for another 4 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The other 4 hours would take you to 3 pm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 15.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the meantime had you discussed the position with your husband, [Father of Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Had you jointly reached the decision that if nothing happened by 3 o'clock you were going to be more forceful as concerned a C-section?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. Yes, I was a bit more -- a bit less patient, absolutely exhausted, and I said, "This is enough now and the next step will be C-section and it's going to happen". Yes, that was it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you reviewed again by the same male doctor, the big guy?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you get the impression that he was more concerned about your situation by 3 pm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Clearly.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And was the information you were given that you were actually -- you'd gone backwards in the sense that you were less dilated than you had been at --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: It seemed more tense and worse than before, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did that doctor confirm that you would be given a Csection?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. He was concerned for me and the baby and he said that it was not a good idea to wait any longer because the baby was going to get distressed and I didn't look in a good state to be delivering naturally.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: From the moment that decision was made, did events develop very much more quickly?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: A lot, because at first everyone was pretty chilled and when he came back and he looked at the note and discussed with the midwife and maybe seen my face, I don't know, and then examined me again, all of a sudden, as soon as he said, "We will do a C-section", things just went very quickly. I was prepared, my husband was scrubbed up and on the way to the theatre.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you were taken to the operating theatre and [Baby D] was delivered?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Anyone who's been at such an occasion or seen one on TV knows there's effectively a screen that separates your top half from your bottom half.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The surgeons work on the other side of the screen.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And was [Baby D] delivered and lifted for you to see over the screen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: She was, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What impression did you get of [Baby D]'s state when you saw her that first time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not alive. She seemed very lifeless. She didn't scream. There was no sound. And everything was quiet in the room.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was there a nurse that you remembered who was in the theatre during this stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you then stitched up?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And were you taken back or up to a ward whilst the medical professionals dealt with [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Where were you when you first had physical contact with your daughter?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: So on the table, they brought her to me and very quickly took her back because she -- they were concerned.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I mean, it seemed a bit rushed, but yes they took her back pretty quickly.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I haven't asked you any questions about this yet, but had you had some form of anaesthetic to remove --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, an epidural.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And how did you feel at this stage? Were you aware of everything that was going on around you, fully aware, partially aware?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Considering -- I'd say I was very aware. I mean, you are in a cross sort of shape, my arms were out, the vision is limited. I don't know -- when they take [Baby D] to the other side, I can't see what's going on, but I think I was quite switched on, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we just be clear because we've reached the stage where [Mother of Baby D] had been taken, she said, back to the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And then you're describing something that happened before you were taken back to the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're back in time so to speak.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: This is after the delivery, before you go back to the ward, and you referred to a table and seeing [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So this was when you were still in the operating theatre?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's my fault for jumping around.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you have physical contact with [Baby D] -- I'll just make sure that we've dealt with everything that happened in the operating theatre. Did you have physical contact with [Baby D] in the operating theatre?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No. Not myself. [Father of Baby D] next to me, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You were taken up to -- was it to an individual room or to a larger room with other people?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: A larger room. There'd been a few people passing, but I would say maybe two or three patients in that room maybe.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And did you have any physical contact with [Baby D] whilst you were in that room, having been taken up from the operating theatre?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I don't believe so. I think I was moved to another room.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Let's deal --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: It was a passing somehow -- when I settled in another room, that's when they brought [Baby D], and I was on my own then.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. Let's just make this absolutely clear. From the operating theatre you were taken to a room where there were two or three other ladies?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I think, yes. It's a bit blurry, this one.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You were moved on to a further room. Was that you alone in the room or with other ladies?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I believe just myself, a couple of midwives and [Father of Baby D].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Was it in that second room that you had physical contact with your daughter, [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What impression did you get of [Baby D]'s condition at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I was really worried because she -- I obviously couldn't move, so they brought her to my chest, so we had skin-to-skin. But she didn't really have any movement, she was quite limp and she didn't have a good colour, she looked a bit grey and then a bit purple, not really an even colour. She seemed to struggle to breathe and she was making those groaning noises. She wasn't really responsive.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was a split second when she sort of opened her eyes a little bit and looked at me -- that's the one picture I've got of her -- and then no response.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I tried to breastfeed her and she was just completely limp, so yes, I was quite worried.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. What were you being told by -- well, did you see a doctor at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: A paediatrician, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And was this paediatrician male or female?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: A male.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What were you told by that male paediatrician at that stage about [Baby D]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: That I didn't need to worry, that she was okay. Her condition's probably due to her being delivered through C-section. So a bit of the breathing wouldn't be as clear. But he didn't seem worried at all.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Were you worried, though, despite what you were being told?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, I didn't believe what he said. I was not happy with his attitude or his -- he seemed just a bit too careless.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: To use a French word, blasé?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Blasé for sure.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you ask for a second opinion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I asked -- there was a few midwives coming in and out of the room. I didn't really understand what was going on and no one was addressing [Baby D]'s condition, and I think [Father of Baby D] was trying to keep me -- as we all know, maybe the hormones kick in and I seemed maybe a bit aggressive and I said, no, there's something wrong with [Baby D] and someone needs to check her. One of the midwives said the doctor confirmed she'll be reassessed in 4 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I said, that's not acceptable, I want another doctor, and someone else who knows what they're doing can come and check her because she's not right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did another doctor come and check [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No. He came back, the same doctor came back, but he'd spoken to a consultant.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you reassured about [Baby D] at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not reassured. I was glad someone took me seriously and took her to be checked out, but I was more worried because then, all of a sudden, from being okay to them, she was taken straight to neonatal intensive care. So I was more worried again.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So far as you were concerned, was it the conversation that the doctor had had -- the paediatrician had had with the consultant that prompted a further examination of
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby D] and then her transfer from your side to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Obviously you were more concerned about [Baby D]. How were you feeling in yourself at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Rubbish. I felt drained. Not relieved from -- I don't know, that was my first birth, but I didn't feel any relief. I felt just in pain, groggy, knackered, you know, not good.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As you remember it, about what time was it that you were separated from [Baby D] and she was removed to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Around 7 or 8, I would say, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in the evening?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So 20 June was a Saturday, I think; do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The following day on the Sunday, 21 June, was that Father's Day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you given any news about [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. She was up and down all night. She was struggling to breathe. She wasn't feeding. But they didn't seem too concerned then, they seemed to think they had things under control, but, yes, she wasn't great at that time.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you remember who it was that was giving you these details?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I don't know the name, but I remember the doctor, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was it a man or a woman?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: A woman.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What was your impression of her status in the hierarchy?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Consultant, registrar or...?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I thought consultant, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you describe her as being in her mid to late 30s?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was she a white lady or not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: She was white, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: British?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: How did you know that, from her accent, the way she spoke? Did English seem to be her first language, in other words?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I'm not sure then, but I would have assumed she was British.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Your physical description of her was, I think, 170 centimetres tall, petite build.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not 170. I would have gone with more average size.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Really average, I'd say, size.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What's your average?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I'd say 165 maybe.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 165, okay. Can you remember what else she told you, if anything, about your daughter?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. So far as [Baby D]'s progress was concerned, what's the next thing that you remember on the Sunday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: She needed to be on a CPAP machine, so the machine was literally breathing for her. They tried to take her off, but every time they did, she would crash. So she still needed that extra help. But they weren't worried because she was -- although she was 3 weeks early, she was a good size baby.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They didn't seem overly concerned. Just she was poorly, but she was doing normal progress, she was doing fine. And the result -- I think they tested -- I don't know what you call them, but they did some blood samples and tests and she seemed fine.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you get to see [Baby D] on the Sunday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Evening.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you remember approximately what time it was that you got to see [Baby D] that Sunday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I'd say around 7.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When you went to see [Baby D], was there a doctor there in the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Had you spoken to a doctor before you went to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you remember that doctor's name?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No. I remember the one just after, so I think we'll get to this one. I don't remember the name of the...
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Which is the name that you can remember?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Dr Brunton.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Brunton, all right. So you saw [Baby D] physically --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- in the neonatal unit? Was she in one of the rooms in the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, it was pretty dark and quiet.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think you drew a diagram of where [Baby D] was. Do you remember drawing that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I just want to show you the diagram on the screen, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can see you have drawn a number of boxes. On your diagram there's a box towards the upper part and the centre upper part of the page as we look at it on screen. Have you drawn within the box, which is the room, the position where you remember [Baby D] being?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Mm-hm, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'd just like to deal with what else we can see there.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Immediately to the left of where the yellow highlight has just been put there's what looks like writing and some lines. What's written there, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you actually draw this?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So everything on here has been written and drawn by you?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: So the room where [Baby D] was, the one next to it, that's not my writing.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: But the...
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Does it say "corner" maybe? I don't know.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: You're right, that is what it is. The room where she was, it was in a corner and it was sort of like a seethrough... That's me recalling, looking into the room to the left, but I don't recall writing what's on that left side. I don't even...
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it may be "room".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: But that's not my writing. The one corner is where [Baby D] was, she was in the corner.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, I was asking the witness about where the cursor is now, that word there.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Corner", underlined many times. Then to the right of that there's a rectangle, a long rectangle with a lot of crosses in it. Do you know what that indicates?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, those were all the machines. There was monitoring of -- I was warned that there would be quite a lot of tubes and things, extra stuff.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And so far as the -- we can see there is a cross above where it says "[Baby D]" and a cross below.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So outside the box with the four crosses in. What are those crosses?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: More -- I don't know the name of them but the things where you have the dripping bit and the IVs.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The stand and that sort of thing?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, all medical things.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's fine. If we could just come out of that closeup, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So whether or not the position of the room is correct in the context of the unit as a whole, that particular room is how you remember the layout in the room when you went down there; is that fair?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I'm pretty certain that is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's get rid of that, please. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You said that you spoke to Dr Brunton.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Where were you when you spoke to Dr Brunton?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: He came to my room, private room.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was that after you had been down to see [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What time was it that you -- or how long after you'd been to see [Baby D] was it that you spoke to Dr Brunton, can you recall?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I would say it was around 9/9.30 in the evening, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. What were you told at that stage about [Baby D]'s situation, her state of health?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: He was very happy with the results of the latest tests.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They've taken blood samples from her belly button rather than the heel. They've done more scans. The jaundice was clearing because she had to have that light treatment thing. She was doing well and he was very hopeful and he promised me that I would be able to hold her and give her a cuddle and feed her the following day and that I could rest, so I was going to rest that night.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Were you reasonably happy at that stage with the overall position?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: For her, yes. I was not in good condition. I was still -- I couldn't walk. I was moved by a wheelchair and I was in 10 out of 10 pain. I was on morphine and I was not in a good state, but for [Baby D], I was happy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When you had seen [Baby D], how did her colour compare to her colour when she been born and the immediate aftermath?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: She looked like a good pink baby, a good healthy colour.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was tiny but she looked chubby, so she looked healthy, she looked okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Following the conversation that you've just told us about that you had with Dr Brunton in your private room, did you see Dr Brunton again?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When did you next see Dr Brunton?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: So... That following night -- [Father of Baby D] was allowed to stay with me non-stop at the hospital, so we both rested and we were woken up around 4.00 in the morning by a nurse who was in panic. She just said, "[Baby D]'s very poorly, you need to come down". We were fast asleep, so just didn't really know what was going on. [Father of Baby D], with the nurse, helped me get on the wheelchair and we rushed downstairs.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Brunton was holding her, trying to -- I can't even say this word, resuscitate.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Resuscitate, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes. He was trying really hard. I couldn't really see [Baby D]. The way he was holding her, I was seeing more of his back, and we were just standing there looking at [Baby D] dying. Someone was holding a phone to his ear and he kept shouting, "This is [Baby D]", and he was quite agitated.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And then Dr Newby told him that he had to let [Baby D] go, he had to stop. And she insisted and she tapped on his shoulder and said, "You've got to let her go", so he held her but he stopped massaging her and he pronounced the time of her death.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I couldn't stay in the room anymore, so then I asked [Father of Baby D] to take me away.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. I just want to -- I know it's difficult, but I just want to break that down a bit, okay? You told the jury that you saw a nurse holding a phone to Dr Brunton's ear.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you know who that nurse was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I think I do.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And who do you think it was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Had you seen Lucy Letby before?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When, prior to this incident at 4.00 in the morning or thereabouts, had you previously seen Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: When I went to see [Baby D] in the neonatal unit, the evening prior, the evening when I went to see her.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So that was at about 7 o'clock, I think you've told us.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When you had walked into the room, how many nurses were in the room with [Baby D] the previous evening?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Just that nurse.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What was going on with [Baby D] when you walked into the room?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Well, that's a question I asked. As I walked — well, not walked in, I was pushed on the wheelchair. As we got in the room, she was sort of hovering around [Baby D] but not doing much. She had a clipboard or something to take notes on. She sort of was looking at the machine, but she didn't -- I didn't really clearly understand what she was doing. I asked if
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: everything was okay and she said, "Yes, she's fine", but then for me that's the first time in 24 hours I could see [Baby D], so I would have expected, once she's done what she needed, our visit was planned, she could have just left us to it and she just stuck around. She sort of was just watching or looking over us and I asked [Father of Baby D], can you tell her to go away or just give us some privacy, and --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Had you heard anything as you'd walked into the room?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Heard anything?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Apart from the sounds of the machines, there was quite a lot of beeping and I'm not familiar with all of them, but there was lines moving and it just seemed like there was a bit too much noise from that, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. So that was your contact with Lucy Letby at about 7 pm on the 21st?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You saw her again at 4 o'clock in the morning --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- as you remember? Was she in the room with you once [Baby D] had passed away?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Came back with us, you mean?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Was she still in the room?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When [Baby D] died was Lucy Letby in the room?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: She was, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was she the only medical professional in the room or were there other doctors and/or nurses there as well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: There was others, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Did there come a stage when the doctors and nurses left the room when [Baby D] had died?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I don't know. We didn't stay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you at a later stage go back to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I don't know if it's classed as the... I mean, it's an area in the children's ward.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes, I went back once she passed, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was [Baby D]'s body there when you went back?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was [Baby D] in a room on her own?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you with your husband, [Father of Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was anybody else in the room?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: [Father of Baby D]'s mum and a nurse that I hadn't seen before.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you ever see Lucy Letby again?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I just have a moment, please, my Lord?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
I wonder whether you'd wait there for some more questions, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
[Mother of Baby D], it is an awful experience that you went through.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I recognise that. And you will know everyone's sympathy is with you and your family. I only have a couple of questions. It won't take long. There's nothing insensitive about it, I just want to check one or two things and then we're done; is that all right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. It's just one matter. You have described that you went down to see [Baby D] at about 7 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that on 21 June?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The Sunday night, all right. Were you with your husband or were you on your own at that time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: With my husband.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I just ask, you seemed clear about 7 o'clock. When I say that, why are you so clear about 7 o'clock, could you just help us with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I must have looked at the clock.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Did you have a conversation with the nurse who was there? I know you say that's Ms Letby, but did you have a conversation with the nurse who was there at all?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: An exchange of a few words.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. I'm going to ask you this and you can agree or disagree as you like. The nurse you were dealing with, is there a possibility that was someone other than Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: I don't think so.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And your view of that, is that because you'd seen Ms Letby's picture in the papers and things and so you were able to pick her out from that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Because -- yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Just wait there one moment, please.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
I said I'd be as quick as I could be, [Mother of Baby D].
That's all I wanted to ask. Thank you very much.
Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. I take it from that that it is disputed that it was her?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, at that time, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just exploring that, you didn't know her name at the time of who this nurse was?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER OF BABY D: Not many names I recall, no.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But it was seeing a picture and then you put a --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

May I read the statement of [Father of Baby D] before we move to the next phase?

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Members of the jury, [Father of Baby D] made a statement dated 25 November 2019, which contains the following:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My daughter, [Baby D], was born at 16.01 hours on Saturday, 20 June 2015 at the Countess of Chester Hospital. She died at 04.25 hours on Monday, 22 June 2015 in the neonatal unit at the hospital. My wife is [Mother of Baby D]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Father of Baby D] says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby D] was our first child. I don't remember any specific problems during [Mother of Baby D]'s pregnancy. From the moment [Baby D] was born, [Mother of Baby D] and I had immediate concerns for her well-being. She didn't behave the way we would expect a newborn baby to be. She didn't seem to cry out loud, groan or be the right colour. She appeared grey.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Initially, we were reassured that she was okay by a paediatrician and other medical staff. As I didn't have any experience of newborn children and their behaviour, I believed what the medical staff were telling me. I was never led at any time to believe that she might die in the circumstances that she did."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He then breaks up his statement as to dates, the first being 18 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D]'s waters broke in the early hours, approximately 4 in the morning, of 18 June 2015. We called the hospital. After explaining [Mother of Baby D]'s condition, we were advised to hang fire and make sure it was her waters that had broken and to monitor any contractions. It was a long time ago, but I don't remember [Mother of Baby D] having any contractions at that specific time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We went to the hospital later that day. I think it was about 10 or 11 o'clock. The nurse that saw us said that it was [Mother of Baby D]'s waters that had broken and confirmed that there were no contractions. [Mother of Baby D] had some checks at this time, but I can't remember what they were or what they were for. We were sent home and [Mother of Baby D] was booked in to be induced the following morning at 08.00 hours."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The next date is 19 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We went back to the hospital on 19 June at about 8 am. We waited a couple of hours to be seen. From memory, the inducement started at about 13.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe that [Mother of Baby D] was given a pessary. We waited, but this did not seem to bring on any contractions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Mother of Baby D] was then given another pessary; I believe this was some time around 5 or 6 in the afternoon. However, once again, this didn't seem to bring on contractions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember that around 11 o'clock, midnight time, [Mother of Baby D] had an injection into one of her hands.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I understood that this was the third phase of inducement. This didn't seem to bring on contractions either."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Next date, 20 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As I remember, [Mother of Baby D] started to have mild contractions between 02.00 and 03.00 hours but still hadn't dilated. At about 7.00 or 8.00, [Mother of Baby D] was encouraged to try another round of the hormone used to bring on contractions and dilation. Again, from memory, there was no movement and [Mother of Baby D] had minimal dilation. I believe that [Mother of Baby D] was checked again at about 11 or midday. Once again, [Mother of Baby D] was encouraged to wait for more progress and to continue with inducement methods.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D] didn't really want to. She felt that she had been in labour a long time since her waters had broken. We were worried about infection and [Mother of Baby D] had not been given any antibiotics at this stage. We did enquire on a number of occasions about antibiotics, but we were told that medical staff were monitoring the situation and there were no signs of an infection and unless there were any abnormalities or any signs of infection, they didn't feel antibiotics were necessary.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D] was assessed again at about 3 in the afternoon. Again, there was still no real dilation. We agreed on a caesarean section, which would have been with immediate effect. Quite soon after, near to 4 o'clock in the afternoon, we went through to the operating theatre for [Mother of Baby D] to have an emergency caesarean section.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once [Baby D] had been delivered, the obstetrician, I think, held [Baby D] up over the sheet momentarily so we could see her. [Baby D] was wrapped up and taken to the scales. We weren't informed that there were any concerns or issues with [Baby D] at this stage and I was led to believe at this time that everything was okay.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I remember that my initial thoughts were that [Baby D] was very quiet. She wasn't as I'd expected a newborn to be.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember [Baby D] was given to me to hold before she took her away. I went over to the scales to cut her cord. I'm not sure if they gave [Baby D] a resuscitation breath of some description or
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: just like a little device at that point, possibly giving her a bit of oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I went back to the room on the labour ward with [Baby D] for a short period of time before [Mother of Baby D] came along and joined us with the midwife. [Mother of Baby D] was given skinto-skin with [Baby D] and we put some pyjamas on her. The midwife assisted [Mother of Baby D] in trying to breastfeed [Baby D]. [Baby D] just didn't seem to be interested in feeding. By this I mean [Baby D] wasn't just having difficulty latching on to the breast, she just didn't seem interested in feeding at all.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We hadn't been informed that [Baby D] had been unwell at any stage. However, given how quiet [Baby D] was and feeling that something wasn't quite right, I remember that we repeatedly asked if she was okay. We just weren't comfortable with how [Baby D] was.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We were reassured each time that [Baby D] was fine.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe that it was a few hours of [Mother of Baby D] expressing concerns before we managed to get another paediatrician to examine [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Later on, around 6 or 7 pm, a different senior paediatrician came to examine [Baby D]. It was a female doctor and she took [Baby D] away to the neonatal ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The female doctor was small/petite, about 5 foot 3 inches, and had short dark hair and wore black-framed glasses, I think.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A short time later, possibly 20.00 hours, this female doctor came back to tell us [Baby D] wasn't very well. I think I went on my own at this time to the neonatal ward to see [Baby D] and it was a bit of a shock.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby D] remained in the neonatal ward over the next 36 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby D] was very poorly in the neonatal ward and was on CPAP breathing equipment. She wasn't feeding and had lots of tubes in her mouth and things on her body, monitoring her. She was also under a lamp for jaundice.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember that the two specially trained neonatal ward staff working in the neonatal ward were called [redacted] and Ailsa. They were both friendly and warm and what you'd expect from nurses working in a baby unit. They comforted me and made sure everything was okay for me. They always made me feel welcome when I went to the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember [Mother of Baby D] was then taken from the labour ward to the maternity ward and I was told I would be able to stay with her overnight. I think [Mother of Baby D] was given some morphine or strong painkillers to help with her pain and I remember she wasn't really coherent after. She was very tired and in pain.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I think about 10 or 10.30 that night one of the doctors from the neonatal ward, Andrew (he was Scottish or Irish) came and introduced himself and to give us a brief update on [Baby D]'s situation."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The next date is 21 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I went down to see [Baby D] and I'm almost certain she was taken off CPAP at some point during the day. My dad came to visit and he also came down to see [Baby D] with me. This would have been in the afternoon, maybe 1 pm or 2 pm. [Mother of Baby D] wasn't really able to visit [Baby D] much, so I visited [Baby D] on my own a lot. I just relied on the staff, really, to give me feedback because I had no understanding of how well or unwell [Baby D] really was.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It was Father's Day and I was given a handmade Father's Day card in the neonatal ward in the afternoon when I went down to visit [Baby D]. The staff had put it together and it was just a brief message on a card which read, 'Happy Father's Day, love [Baby D]'. There was a photo of [Baby D] stuck inside.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On the first photograph she is on CPAP and has tubes and wires on her. I took that card away with me.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Later in the day, I think, I was given a welcome card and the photo of [Baby D] on the card shows her looking a lot healthier and showing signs of getting better.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She's not on CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He then goes on to say:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember that at some point we got a call to ask if [Baby D] could be given donor milk. We were happy for this to happen and I left [Mother of Baby D]'s bedside and went to the neonatal ward to give consent. I took the opportunity to see [Baby D]. I think the time would have been between 22.30 hours and 23.59 hours. I can't remember if I had to sign a consent form or if it was just verbal consent."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The next date, 22 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We were woken in the early hours of the morning.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The midwife told us that we needed to go down to the neonatal ward as [Baby D] was poorly. [Mother of Baby D] and I were taken to the neonatal ward by a midwife from the maternity ward. [Mother of Baby D] was in a wheelchair and someone met us to open the doors to the neonatal ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There was a quick handover with the neonatal ward staff.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When we walked into the room, we understood immediately it was a very serious situation. When we walked in the ward, there were lots of medical staff around [Baby D]. Andrew, the doctor, seemed to be in charge at that particular time. That's the way it appeared.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember someone mentioning adrenaline and just a real sense of urgency. I remember Andrew had a phone held to his ear by another member of staff and he was just discussing the situation with the person on the other end of the phone. He was trying to explain who the baby was. It sounded to me like there was some confusion over which baby they were talking about.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Andrew was saying something similar to, 'No, no, not [a name], it's [Baby D]'.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The person on the other end of the phone didn't seem to understand it was [Baby D]. They thought it was another child. I don't remember the name but he said, 'No, not [such-and-such], it's [Baby D]'.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "They were unsuccessful in resuscitating [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Newby came to inform us that [Baby D] had died. She said that they had been trying to resuscitate [Baby D] for over 20 minutes. I think Dr Newby had to tell Andrew to stop. It just wasn't successful and Dr Newby seemed shocked and upset. I couldn't tell you which staff were in the operating theatre when [Baby D] was being resuscitated as I didn't pay a great deal of attention to what they were doing. I didn't want to look and I just know that there was a number of staff around [Baby D]. I don't even know if Dr Newby was in the room when we arrived or if she arrived during [Baby D]'s resuscitation as I didn't really look in that direction.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I could hear the severity of the situations in people's voices.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We weren't in the room a long time, perhaps 5 minutes. They had been trying to resuscitate [Baby D] prior to our arrival and when they realised how serious the situation was, they contacted the ward for us to go down. I don't recall seeing Lucy Letby at this time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We went to the maternity ward and I rang family to let them know what had happened."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Can I just interrupt you there? There's a reference to staff in the operating theatre. I don't think there's any issue in relation to this. It means the room in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, nursery 1 where these events were taking place.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Father of Baby D] then gives an account of his recollection of the events after [Baby D]'s passing, which aren't relevant to the issues that you need to consider, members of the jury. Then his statement reflects on some of the previous comings and goings and he says this at page 11 of 16, my Lord:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I can't be specific about how often I went down and saw [Baby D]. I went quite frequently, popping in and out during the day, and would sit with her for an hour or so at a time. I was never given the impression that [Baby D]'s condition was lifethreatening and it didn't even cross my mind that she was in danger of dying.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As far as I was led to believe, babies get infections all the time and there was nothing unusual about that. When she died, we just were not prepared for it, and [Mother of Baby D] was struggling to come down to see her because she had a C-section and was in a lot of pain.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst I sat with [Baby D], I would observe nurses coming and going, doing checks and nothing that I saw appeared out of the ordinary, but I don't know really what they were doing or why as I had nothing to compare their actions to.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I can confirm that I was never present when [Baby D]'s health deteriorated or were phoned to receive such information."
